title: THEY PROPHESIED, CAST OUT DEMONS, AND DID MIRACLES—SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
paragraphs: THEY PROPHESIED, CAST OUT DEMONS, AND DID MIRACLES—SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?

The most terrifying words in Matthew 7 were not spoken to atheists who wanted nothing to do with Jesus. They were spoken about people who called Him “Lord,” performed extraordinary works in His name, and apparently expected heaven—only to discover that knowing about the power of Jesus is not the same thing as belonging to Jesus.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every person who calls himself a Christian go quiet.
Not because Jesus whispers it to someone who hated Him.
Not because He says it to someone who spent his entire life mocking Christianity.
Not because the people standing before Him had never heard His name.
Quite the opposite.
They knew His name.
They called Him Lord.
They spoke in His name.
They claimed supernatural works in His name.
And apparently, right up until the moment Jesus answered them, they believed their spiritual résumé meant something.
Then Christ said:
“I never knew you.”
Read that again.
Not, “I knew you once.”
Not, “I knew you until you made too many mistakes.”
Not, “You weren't impressive enough.”
“I never knew you.”
And suddenly Matthew 7:21–23 becomes more than a warning about “those fake Christians out there.”
It becomes a mirror.
Jesus says:
“Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι· Κύριε κύριε…”
Ou pas ho legōn moi, Kyrie kyrie…
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord’…”
The Greek Κύριε, κύριε — Kyrie, kyrie is emphatic. These people are addressing Jesus as Lord. Their mouths contain orthodox-sounding language. Their defense is not, “Jesus, we rejected You.”
Their defense is essentially:
Jesus, look at everything we did for You.
That is what makes the passage so disturbing.
Because the people Jesus describes are not spiritually indifferent.
They are spiritually impressive.
“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name?”
“Did we not cast out demons in Your name?”
“Did we not do many mighty works in Your name?”
Imagine hearing those words without knowing what comes next.
You might expect Jesus to say:
“Well done.”
Instead, the Judge of humanity answers:
“καὶ τότε ὁμολογήσω αὐτοῖς ὅτι Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς…”
Kai tote homologēsō autois hoti oudepote egnōn hymas…
“And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you.’”
The word translated “never” is οὐδέποτε — oudepote.
Never.
At no time.
And the verb translated “knew” is ἔγνων — egnōn, from γινώσκω — ginōskō, “to know.”
Jesus' point is not that He lacked information about these people. The One presented in this very passage as the final Judge obviously isn't saying, “I don't recognize your face.”
This is relational language.
They could use His name while never truly belonging to Him.
They could speak about Him while remaining strangers to Him.
They could build a public identity around Jesus while their hearts remained unsubmitted to Jesus.
And perhaps that is the question this passage forces into places we would rather keep locked:
What if people know you as a Christian, but Christ does not know you as His?
You can know worship songs.
You can know Christian vocabulary.
You can repost sermons.
You can argue theology.
You can own six Bibles.
You can serve at church.
You can cry during worship.
You can say “God told me.”
You can have thousands of followers listening to you talk about Jesus.
You can preach.
You can lead.
You can build ministries.
You can become known for Christianity…
…and still need Christ.
That is not meant to drive the genuine believer into endless neurotic terror, forever wondering whether one more failure has erased the grace of God.
It is meant to destroy something far more dangerous:
false assurance.
Because Jesus does not tell us to place our confidence in religious performance.
In fact, look carefully at the defense of these people.
“Did we not prophesy?”
“Did we not cast out demons?”
“Did we not perform many mighty works?”
Their final argument is a list of accomplishments.
But no sinner will enter the Kingdom because his résumé impressed the King.
The Gospel has never been:
“Look what I did for Jesus.”
The Gospel begins with:
Look what Jesus did for sinners.

The Son of God came for people who could never rescue themselves. He lived without sin. He gave Himself for sinners. He bore sin at the cross. He died and rose again. Forgiveness is not wages paid to impressive religious people; it is grace received through faith in Christ.
So Matthew 7 cannot mean, “Perform enough good works and Jesus will finally accept you.”
That would contradict the Gospel.
Jesus is exposing something else.
He says in Matthew 7:21 that the person who enters the Kingdom is the one who does “τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου” — to thelēma tou patros mou — “the will of My Father.”
Then in verse 23 He describes those He rejects as:
“οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν”
hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian
“those practicing lawlessness.”
The word ἀνομία — anomia carries the sense of lawlessness, disregard for God's righteous rule.
Notice the contrast.
Jesus does not contrast “people who perform miracles” with “people who perform even bigger miracles.”
He contrasts outward claims with obedience.
Profession with reality.
Spectacle with fruit.
A mouth saying “Lord” with a life refusing His lordship.
And that makes even more sense when you refuse to rip verses 21–23 away from their context.
Just before these words, Jesus warns about false prophets who come appearing harmless but are inwardly ravenous.
Then He says:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
Fruit.
Not fame.
Fruit.
Not followers.
Fruit.
Not supernatural stories.
Fruit.
Not platform size.
Fruit.
Not how loudly someone says “Jesus.”
Fruit.
Jesus' warning is devastating precisely because spectacular gifts are not the same thing as godly character.
A person may attract attention without displaying holiness.
A person may know how to move a crowd without knowing how to kneel privately before God.
A person may preach repentance publicly while protecting secret sin privately.
A person may become skilled at looking anointed while becoming comfortable with what crucified Christ.
And this is where the article must stop being about somebody else.
Because it is easy to read Matthew 7 and immediately think of the preacher you distrust.
The celebrity pastor who fell.
The hypocrite who hurt you.
The religious relative who lives differently on Monday.
The person online whose Christianity seems fake.
But Jesus did not give us this passage so we could comfortably use it as binoculars.
Sometimes Scripture is a mirror.
So forget everybody else for a moment.
What happens when nobody is watching you?
What are you protecting that you would be ashamed to bring into the light?
What sin have you renamed so you don't have to repent of it?
What bitterness have you baptized as “discernment”?
What lust have you excused as weakness while refusing to fight it?
What dishonesty have you called survival?
What pride have you disguised as confidence?
What unforgiveness have you defended because the person really did hurt you?
What secret life exists underneath your public Christianity?
And before shame convinces you to run away from God, hear this carefully:
Jesus exposes darkness because He calls sinners into light.
Conviction is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come.
That is why the answer to Matthew 7 is not pretending harder.
It is not performing harder.
It is not panicking until you have accumulated enough spiritual accomplishments to feel safe again.
It is coming honestly to Jesus Christ.
Repenting.
Believing.
Surrendering.
Receiving mercy you could never earn.
Because the same Christ whose words terrify the hypocrite is the Christ who welcomes the repentant sinner.
That distinction matters.
Peter failed Jesus spectacularly.
Peter denied that he even knew Him.
Three times.
Yet Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
Why?
Because Christianity is not the story of flawless people maintaining flawless records.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a flawless Savior.
Judas could stand near Jesus and remain hardened.
Peter could collapse in failure and be restored.
The difference was not that Peter's sin was cute.
It wasn't.
The difference was that grace brought a broken sinner back to Christ.
That is what Jesus does.
He rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until sin becomes harmless.
He rewrites the story by taking guilty people who deserve judgment and giving forgiveness to those who come to Him in repentant faith.
And Scripture gives us another chilling scene that prevents us from treating the name of Jesus like a religious formula.
In Acts 19, some itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of Jesus over evil spirits. The sons of Sceva were among those doing this.
They had heard the Name.
They tried to use the Name.
But they did not possess a magical formula.
The evil spirit answered:
“Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?”
The attempt ended disastrously.
And when Ephesus heard what happened, something remarkable followed.
The name of Jesus was not diminished.
It was magnified.
People came confessing their practices. Those involved in magic brought their books and publicly burned them.
In other words, genuine encounter with the authority of Christ produced something counterfeit spirituality does not want:
repentance.
The name of Jesus is not an incantation.
Christianity is not spiritual magic.
Jesus is not a tool for getting power, money, influence, healing, attention, success, followers, miracles, or a better life.
He is Lord.
And perhaps one of the greatest dangers in modern Christianity is wanting everything Jesus can give while resisting Jesus Himself.
We want peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Heaven without holiness.
Promises without obedience.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A Savior who rescues us from consequences but never confronts our idols.
But biblical grace does not merely pardon.
Grace transforms.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without battles.
Not without falls, tears, confession, discipline, and desperate prayers.
But genuinely.
A person rescued by Christ does not become sinless in this life, but he cannot make peace with sin as though Christ died merely to make rebellion comfortable.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and settling down with it.
One says:
“Jesus, I hate that I keep falling. Have mercy on me. Change me. Help me fight.”
The other says:
“I know what God says. I simply intend to keep doing what I want.”
One falls while facing toward Christ.
The other wants Christ's benefits while reserving the throne.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you know you have failed Him, don't misunderstand the warning.
Your tears do not disqualify you from grace.
Your past does not place you beyond the blood of Christ.
Your secret is not stronger than His mercy.
Your scandal is not bigger than His cross.
The question is not whether you have ever sinned.
We all have.
The question is what you will do when Christ brings your sin into the light.
Hide?
Excuse it?
Defend it?
Rename it?
Blame somebody else?
Or fall before Jesus and say:
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
There is mercy there.
Real mercy.
Not cheap mercy.
Blood-bought mercy.
The kind purchased at a Roman cross where the innocent Son of God suffered for guilty sinners.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride dies because you cannot save yourself.
Despair dies because Christ saves sinners.
You cannot boast:
“Look what I have done.”
But you also do not have to whisper:
“I have gone too far.”
At Calvary, the answer to both is Jesus.
Jesus.
Jesus.
That is why the most important question of your life is not:
“Do people think I'm Christian?”
Not:
“Have I had spiritual experiences?”
Not:
“Did I grow up in church?”
Not:
“Was I baptized?”
Not:
“Can I quote Scripture?”
Not even:
“Have I done ministry?”
The question beneath all of those questions is terrifyingly personal:
Do I belong to Jesus Christ?
You may forget this article.
You may forget the person who shared it.
You may forget half the sentences you just read.
But please do not forget:
“I never knew you.”
Those words are too serious to gamble eternity on appearances.
Examine yourself honestly.
Run to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Abandon what needs abandoning.
Forgive where you need to forgive.
Make restitution where repentance requires it.
Open the locked room.
Bring the secret into the light.
And trust Christ rather than your religious résumé.
If you are exhausted from fighting sin and afraid your repeated failures mean Jesus wants nothing more to do with you, remember: the answer is not to run from Him.
Run to Him.
The Savior who warned us in Matthew 7 is the Savior who went to the cross for sinners.
Maybe your prayer tonight doesn't need impressive words.
Maybe it is simply:

“Jesus, I don't want to perform Christianity anymore. Search me. Expose what is false in me. Forgive me. Save me. Change me. Teach me to obey You because I belong to You. I have nothing to boast about except Your mercy.”
And if that is where your heart is right now, don't make this another emotional moment that disappears tomorrow morning.
Stay near Scripture.
Stay near Christ.
Find a faithful Bible-teaching church.
Pray when nobody applauds.
Repent when nobody knows.
Obey when obedience costs something.
Love people who cannot increase your platform.
Serve when nobody records it.
Give when nobody praises it.
Forgive when your flesh wants revenge.
And when you fail, confess it instead of constructing another mask.
That quiet life may never look spectacular on social media.
But the Kingdom of God was never built around looking spectacular.
Somebody hiding in the same darkness you once knew may need to discover that Jesus still restores sinners.
Don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because clicking “share” proves you are saved. It doesn't.
But if this truth has helped you, sharing it is one simple way you can glorify God by putting His Word in front of someone who may desperately need to hear it.
Send it privately to someone if publicly tagging them would embarrass them.
Because one day, the applause stops.
The platforms disappear.
The titles mean nothing.
The crowds are gone.
There is no microphone.
No follower count.
No reputation to hide behind.
No ministry résumé to hand Jesus.
Only you…
and the King.
And on that day, the greatest miracle will not be that your name was known by thousands of people.
It will be that the sinner who had every reason to hide finally ran to Jesus—and discovered that grace had been calling them home.
